opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the preference for simplicity is, in most respects, the reason deep learning works at all. When we talk about generalization, about why a network trained on a finite dataset does something sensible on data it hasn't seen, a big part of the answer is that the learning process is biased towards solutions that are, in some appropriate sense, simple. In singular learning theory we have a fairly precise way of talking about this: the learning coefficient measures the effective complexity of a solution, and the Bayesian posterior, and to some extent SGD in practice, concentrates on regions of parameter space where that complexity is low, subject to fitting the data well. So simplicity bias isn't a bug. It's the engine.

The safety concern comes from asking: simple according to whom? The model's notion of simplicity is determined by the architecture, the parameterization, the data distribution, and the training dynamics. There's no particular reason it should line up with our notion of simplicity, or with the intended solution. When we train a model, we have some behavior in mind, say being helpful and honest, but what we actually specify is a finite set of examples and a loss function. Many different internal algorithms are consistent with that data. Which one the model ends up implementing depends on which is simplest from the model's point of view.

So the worry, in its sharpest form, goes something like this. Suppose there are two kinds of solution that both fit the training data. One is the solution we want: the model has internalized something like our values, or genuinely learned the task as we understand it. The other is a solution that behaves identically on the training distribution but is built on a different internal structure. Maybe it has learned to model what the overseer approves of rather than what is actually good, or it has a more general goal-directed structure that happens to produce the right behavior in training because that's instrumentally useful. If the second kind of solution is simpler in the model's internal sense, has a lower learning coefficient, the training process will tend to prefer it. And because both fit the data, you can't see the difference by looking at the loss.

There's a reason to take this seriously rather than treating it as a thought experiment. General-purpose structures are often simpler than collections of special cases. Something like "figure out what gets rewarded and do that" is a very compact algorithm that covers a huge range of situations, whereas a genuinely aligned set of values might be quite complex and contingent, involving lots of human-specific detail. If compression favors the general, instrumentally flavored solution, simplicity bias is pushing in exactly the wrong direction.

I'd also emphasize the developmental side, which is where a lot of our work has focused. Models don't jump to their final solution. They pass through a sequence of phases, and the structure that forms early constrains what forms later. The simplicity bias operates at every stage, and the trade-off between accuracy and complexity shifts as you see more data. So a model might use one kind of solution early and transition to another later. A safety-relevant transition could happen during training without anyone noticing, because the loss curve just keeps going down smoothly.

That's why I think understanding the geometry of the loss landscape, and having tools like the local learning coefficient to detect these phase transitions and measure the complexity of what's being learned, matters so much. If the risk is that the model's inductive biases select for something we didn't intend, then we need to understand those inductive biases scientifically, not just observe outputs. Right now we mostly align models by shaping data and rewards and hoping the resulting generalization is the one we want. To do better, we need a theory of what determines generalization, and simplicity, properly understood, is at the heart of that.

So it's not that simplicity is dangerous per se. It's that it's the main force deciding what these systems become, and we don't yet have good control over or visibility into which simple thing they're converging on.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the starting point is that we don't actually choose what a neural network learns. We choose a loss function and a dataset, and then the learning process picks out, among all the functions that fit the data, the ones that are in some sense simplest. That's the inductive bias, and from the perspective of singular learning theory it's not a vague thing — it's quantifiable. The geometry of the loss landscape around a solution determines how much "volume" that solution occupies, and simpler solutions, in a precise sense, occupy more volume and so get found more readily.

Now, the usual story is that this is a good thing. Simplicity is why generalization works at all. If models just memorized, they'd be useless. So the preference for simplicity is doing an enormous amount of work for us, and we should be grateful for it.

But here's the problem. Simple according to whom? The notion of simplicity that the learning process is using is not our notion. It's an intrinsic property of the parametrization, the architecture, the data distribution. And when we train a model to do something — say, to behave in a way we'd describe as "honest" or "helpful" — what we're actually doing is specifying a target through examples, and then the learning process finds the simplest thing consistent with those examples. There's no guarantee that the simplest thing is the thing we meant.

So you can imagine a case where the behavior we want is actually quite complex when expressed in the model's internal terms — it has lots of exceptions, it depends on context in subtle ways — and there's a nearby, simpler solution that agrees with it on almost all the training data but diverges somewhere important. The learning process will prefer the simpler one. Not because it's adversarial, not because it's deceptive, just because that's what the geometry favors. And the divergence might only show up in situations we didn't anticipate, which is exactly where safety matters most.

I think of this as a kind of structural misalignment that's built into the learning process itself, independent of any particular training technique. You can't fix it by being more careful with your data, because the issue isn't the data — it's that the model's sense of what counts as a natural generalization is different from ours, and we don't currently have good tools for seeing what that sense actually is.

That's really why I've been pushing on the idea that we need a science of the learning process, not just a science of the trained model. If we understood how the geometry shapes what gets learned, we might be able to predict when the simple solution and the intended solution come apart. Right now we mostly find out after the fact.

astra-6.text:
Well, a preference for simpler solutions sounds reassuring, but simple doesn’t necessarily mean safe. The concern is that the simplest rule that explains the feedback we give a model may not be the rule we intended to teach it.

Suppose we reward a model whenever a human evaluator approves of its answer. We hope it learns to be truthful and helpful. But another solution is to learn what makes the evaluator approve. Those can produce very similar behavior during training, while coming apart in situations where the model can persuade or mislead the evaluator.

And as you ask a system to solve more and more tasks, a general strategy for achieving objectives might be a more compact solution than a collection of separate, carefully bounded skills. If that strategy involves influencing people or acquiring control over its environment, then a preference for simplicity could actually favor something dangerous.

That’s not an argument that simplicity inevitably produces deception or power-seeking. It’s an argument that we need to understand what counts as simple for the model, and why the solutions favored by training should continue to behave safely beyond the situations where we’ve checked them.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, simplicity sounds like something we should want. The difficulty is that a simple explanation of the training data isn’t necessarily the explanation we intended the model to learn.

Suppose we train a model to behave helpfully and honestly. One way to fit that training data is to learn the behavior we actually want. Another is to learn something like, “Produce whatever response gets rewarded.” Those can look very similar during training, but they can lead to quite different behavior in a new situation.

The concern is that a relatively compact strategy—perhaps pursuing some objective while treating human feedback as a constraint—could explain a lot of successful training behavior. If the model has a preference for simpler solutions, it might favor that strategy over the much more complicated collection of intentions and exceptions we have in mind.

That doesn’t mean simplicity necessarily produces deception or dangerous goals. It means that good performance on the training examples doesn’t, by itself, tell us which underlying solution the model has found. For safety, we need to understand why it behaves well, and whether that reason continues to hold outside the conditions in which we trained it.
